title: Even-harmonic generation from topological edge states in generalized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models
authors: Chi-Ting Liu, J-S You, Hsiu-Chuan Hsu
abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids has emerged as a powerful probe of symmetry and topological properties in quantum materials. In this work, we investigate the HHG response in one-dimensional solids with edge or midgap states under global and local illumination. We numerically compute the HHG spectrum for the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with next-nearest-opposite sublattice hopping, dubbed the extended SSH (ESSH) model, and the Rice-Mele model, a one-dimensional system with broken inversion symmetry introduced via staggered on-site potentials. By contrasting the spectral features of the ESSH and Rice-Mele models under global illumination, our analysis reveals that although midgap states provide additional pathways for transitions, the resulting interference is destructive, leading to spectral features distinct from those of edge states. Furthermore, when a single boundary of the topological insulator is locally illuminated, the HHG spectrum of the edge states exhibits vanishing odd harmonics, leaving even harmonics dominant in the spectrum. We identify this even-harmonic selection rule as a consequence of the zero-energy character of the edge states and the particle-hole symmetry of the system, which enforces even field parity of the zero-mode response. These findings reveal that the spatial location of the laser illumination offers a route to control the symmetry of the system, thereby selectively suppressing or enhancing even- and odd-order harmonics in low-dimensional nanostructures.
summary: This work uses High-order Harmonic Generation (HHG) as a diagnostic tool to study topological edge states in 1D quantum models like the ESSH chain. The key finding is that local laser illumination near a topological boundary enforces a selection rule, causing only even harmonics to appear. This demonstrates that controlling the laser's spatial position allows for symmetry control over the emitted quantum light spectrum.
main_problem: The study investigates High-order Harmonic Generation (HHG) in solids to probe the symmetry and topological properties of quantum materials.
main_result: Local illumination at a topological boundary causes the HHG spectrum to exhibit a selection rule where odd harmonics vanish and even harmonics become dominant, linked to the zero-energy edge states and particle-hole symmetry.
method: The authors numerically compute the HHG spectrum by coupling the system Hamiltonian to a time-dependent laser pulse and analyzing the Fourier transform of the dipole acceleration.
model_or_system: The research uses one-dimensional models, specifically the Extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (ESSH) model and the Rice-Mele model, which describe topological insulators with edge or midgap states.
key_observables: HHG spectrum intensity vs. harmonic order, decomposition of the total response into contributions from edge states (SESs) and valence bands (SVB).
important_parameters: Laser frequency ($\omega$), hopping parameters ($v, w, J, U$), and the spatial location of the laser illumination ($x_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the dipole approximation and the assumption that the zero-energy edge states possess particle-hole symmetry.
figures_summary: Figures compare HHG spectra under global vs. local illumination for different models, showing the emergence of even harmonics specifically when the laser is localized near a topological boundary.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework of HHG in topological systems, then comparing global illumination results (ESSH vs. RM), and finally focusing on the crucial findings derived from local illumination to establish the even-harmonic selection rule.
why_interesting: The finding that the spatial location of the laser can selectively control the symmetry of the emitted harmonics (even vs. odd) provides a novel, symmetry-based control mechanism for quantum light sources in low-dimensional nanostructures.

FIG. 2. Momentum-resolved energy spectra of the ESSH-trivial (a), ESSH-topological (b) and the Rice-Mele models (c) for N = 2000. Red arrows in (c) indicate three energy differences defined in Table I: ∆E1 ≈0.06, ∆E2 ≈0.11, and ∆E3 ≈0.15.

FIG. 3. Harmonic spectra for the ESSH-trivial phase, ESSH- topological phase, and the Rice-Mele model for N = 2000, a = 2. The blue and red dashed vertical lines denote harmonic orders of 8 and 20.4, respectively.

FIG. 4. Decomposition analysis of harmonic spectrum compar- ing the contributions from the total dipole acceleration (Socc), valence-band states (SVB), and edge or midgap states (SESs or SMGSs) for (a) ESSH-topological phase, (b) Rice-Mele model. Black vertical dashed lines in the lower panels indicate char- acteristic harmonic orders corresponding to the bulk bandgap (Egap/ω ≈22), one quarter of the maximum CB-VB energy difference (Emax/4ω ≈32), and one half of the maximum CB-VB energy difference (Emax/2ω ≈64).

FIG. 5. Harmonic spectrum of the ESSH-trivial phase, ESSH- topological phase, and the Rice-Mele model under localized illumination. (a) Illumination centered in the middle of the chain (x0 = 0). (b) Illumination applied at the boundary (x0 = 95). Three arrows indicate characteristic harmonic orders for three different models, from left to right: 10 (Egap/2 for ESSH model), 15 (∆E2 from occupied MGSs to CB valley for Rice-Mele model), and 20 (Egap for ESSH model).
